assessable_statement_group: Food animals use energy for movement and maintaining body temperature as well as growth. Reducing movement or controlling the surroundings can reduce some energy transfers, leaving more of a supplied intake available for growth. assessable_statement_group: Fish stocks in many ocean fisheries have declined. Overfishing can reduce stocks until too few breeding fish remain. Continuing breeding is important for maintaining populations, and a species may disappear from a local area even while it exists elsewhere. Sustainable management aims to support future stocks and catches, not simply maximise the present catch.

assessable_statement_group: A suitable larger mesh can allow smaller juvenile fish to escape, giving them a chance to grow and breed. Quotas restrict the permitted catch. Mesh size changes which fish are caught; a quota controls how much catch is allowed. Neither alone guarantees recovery, because compliance, species biology, bycatch and environmental conditions also matter.

assessable_statement_group: Our toy stock starts with 40 juveniles and 60 adults. The chosen adult catch is 20 or 60. Small mesh adds 10 juvenile bycatch outside that adult target; large mesh adds none. After the catch, new juveniles equal half the remaining adults in this fictional step. Add survivors and recruits to get the next total. This is not a real quota rule or a calibrated stock forecast.

assessable_statement_group: With adult catch 20, next totals are 90 with small mesh and 100 with large mesh. Catch 60 leaves no breeding adults: next totals 30 or 40, even though some juveniles remain. The model omits maturation, immigration, natural deaths and density dependence. Longer-term survey data and reproductive biology are needed; a one-cycle total is not proof of permanent sustainability.
